sections.text:
Ecclesiastes records the reflections of a speaker called the Teacher. He examines work, pleasure, wealth and wisdom and finds that none of them lasts or satisfies. His repeated word for this is often translated vanity; it pictures a breath or a vapour.

Alongside that hard look, the book keeps returning to simple gifts: food, work and companionship received from God’s hand. It closes with a call to fear God and keep his commandments.

The Teacher is introduced as a son of David and king in Jerusalem, and tradition identifies him with Solomon. Many scholars think the Hebrew of the book points to a later date. A narrator frames the Teacher’s words at the beginning and the end.

Readers differ on the Teacher’s tone. Some hear a skeptic whose view the closing verses correct. Others hear a realist who shows honestly what life looks like when it is measured only by what can be seen. Christians often read the book as clearing the ground: it exposes what cannot bear the weight of a life, and so points beyond itself.
